To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the presence of high concentrations of toxic metals in the water samples of Matanza River did not always produce toxic effects on P. subcapitiata.

the toxicity of the dissolved fraction (< 1.2 μm) of the Matanza River to the freshwater alga Pseudikirchneriella sp. is mainly due to free ionic forms (FIFs) of Pb and Zn, and the presence of organic compounds that reduce metal bioavailability.

the toxicity of metals in water samples of an Argentinean urban river was mainly related with the presence of free ionic metal species in dissolved fraction, which was also related to the physicochemical characteristics of water samples.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

toxicity of metal-contaminated water samples to the green algal P. subcapita is not only related to total metal concentrations, but also to their chemical speciation and to the presence of other organic and inorganic ligands in the water.
toxicity in the river water samples was mainly related to the presence free ionic forms (Cd, Cu and Zn) in the dissolved fraction.
metal contamination of the studied river is mainly related to the presence and bioavailability of Cu and Zn.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the toxic potential for the green alga was mainly associated to the free ionic forms, but other chemical speciation could be also involved.
the toxicity of metals in the water samples of the Matanza-Riachielo River could not be related with the presence of toxic metals in the dissolved fraction.

toxicity of metals in water samples of Matanza-Riachielo River is related to the free ionic concentrations of Pd or Cu, whereas toxicity of Zn is related to the presence or absence of organic ligands.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the toxicity of metals in aquatic ecosystems is not only related to their concentrations, but also to the physicochemical forms of the contaminants.
the toxicity assessment in aquatic ecosystems must include a detailed characterization of metal bioavailability, as a function of the chemical speciation and size fractionation.
the toxicity of heavy metals in water samples from urban rivers can be predicted by considering the bioavailability of metals, which is highly influenced by chemical speciation.
